core: Working definition of crime: behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions
Crime versus deviance: illegal versus norm-violating (deviance is a sibling topic, referenced only at the boundary)
Types of crime: violent, property (nonviolent), white-collar (corporate), and debated victimless crimes
Who is counted: police-based data (FBI UCR) and survey data (BJS NCVS); not all crime is reported
Social patterns: crime rates vary by place, age, and circumstance
Honest note on fear: public fear of crime can outrun the official data
Honest framing: crime statistics are a social mirror reflecting what societies record, report, and ask about
supporting: Legal codes as formal social control maintained by a political authority
Why crimes go unreported (fear, shame, distrust of police, belief that nothing would be done)
Long-term decline in U.S. violent and property crime rates from the early 1990s to the early 2020s, with year-to-year bumps
White-collar crime can do more financial damage than street crime while drawing less media attention
outOfScope: Deviance theory and the labeling of deviance (sibling topic sociology:foundations:deviance)
Social control theory and sanctions systems (sibling topic sociology:foundations:social-control)
Criminal law doctrine, elements of offenses, and sentencing law (law subject)
Criminal psychology, offender psychology, and profiling (psychology subject)
Criminal justice system operations: policing, courts, corrections, and incarceration statistics
Policy positions on crime, policing, or punishment

claims.claim: Crime is a behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions; deviance, by contrast, is a violation of social norms.
Societies maintain legal codes, rules adopted and enforced by a political authority, and those who violate them incur negative formal sanctions.

Violent crimes are based on the use of force or the threat of force (e.g., murder, rape, armed robbery); nonviolent or property crimes involve the destruction or theft of property without force (e.g., larceny, car theft, vandalism).

White-collar (corporate) crime is committed by white-collar workers in a business environment, such as embezzlement, insider trading, and identity theft, and can be more financially damaging than street crime while receiving less media coverage.

Victimless crime is a debated category: illegal acts in which the person committing them is not explicitly harming anyone else (e.g., underage drinking, selling a sexual act), with critics arguing such acts do harm society; the label is contested, not settled.
The FBI's Uniform Crime Reports (UCR) compile data on crimes reported to law enforcement from thousands of police agencies; the UCR does not capture crimes that go unreported.

The Bureau of Justice Statistics' National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is an annual survey of a nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households, ages 12 and older, and captures victimizations both reported and not reported to police.

Not all crime is reported to police: in 2022, only 41.5% of violent crimes and 31.8% of household property crimes were reported, with victims citing fear of reprisal, reluctance to get the offender in trouble, doubt that police would help, or a view of the crime as too trivial or personal.

U.S. violent and property crime rates fell sharply from the early 1990s to the early 2020s: FBI data show the violent crime rate down 49% and the property crime rate down 59% between 1993 and 2022, with BJS data showing even steeper declines; notable year-to-year increases (e.g., murder in 2020) occurred within the long-term decline.

Violent victimization varies by age, income, and place: in the 2022 BJS survey, younger people and lower-income people were far more likely than older and higher-income people to report violent victimization; in 2022 FBI data, violent crime rates exceeded 700 per 100,000 residents in New Mexico and Alaska but were below 200 per 100,000 in Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Hampshire, and Maine.

Fear of crime can outrun the data: in 23 of 27 Gallup surveys since 1993, at least 60% of U.S. adults said there was more crime nationally than the year before, despite declining official crime rates during most of that period.

No single U.S. measure captures all crime: the UCR misses unreported crimes and uneven agency participation, while the NCVS cannot count murder and misses people without stable addresses; the two sources are best read together as a partial, socially produced picture.

conflictingEvidence.issue: NCVS sample size differs between sources: OpenStax 7.3 cites about 160,000 respondents per year, while the BJS NCVS overview page (current) cites about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households.
positions: OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e, section 7.3: approximately 160,000 people surveyed each year (figure from an earlier survey year)
Bureau of Justice Statistics NCVS overview (read live 2026-08-22): nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the BJS figures (240,000 persons / 150,000 households), since BJS is the primary authority for its own survey and the figure reflects the current survey design; the older OpenStax figure is not repeated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Long-term decline versus recent increases: crime rates fell sharply since the early 1990s, yet the U.S. murder rate saw its largest single-year increase on record in 2020 and remained elevated into 2022.
positions: Long-term trend: FBI and BJS data both show large declines in violent and property crime rates from 1993 to 2022
Short-term movement: murder rose sharply in 2020 within that long-term decline
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the long-term decline with attributed FBI/BJS numbers and notes that year-to-year bumps occur, avoiding both scare framing and the false claim of steady decline.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The victimless crime category is contested: some argue acts like underage drinking or selling a sexual act harm no one but the actor; others argue they harm society (e.g., through abuse or workplace consequences).
positions: Crimes may be called victimless when the perpetrator is not explicitly harming another person
Critics argue such acts do harm society and should not be called victimless
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents victimless crime as a debated category, not a settled legal or sociological fact, exactly as OpenStax 7.3 frames it.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. openstax.org blocks direct automated fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20260422203510/..., captured 2026-04-22). Supports: the working definition of crime (behavior that violates official law, punishable through formal sanctions) and the deviance/crime distinction (deviance = violation of social norms); legal codes as rules adopted and enforced by a political authority with negative formal sanctions; the violent/nonviolent (property) crime distinction with named examples; corporate (white-collar) crime (embezzlement, insider trading, identity theft) and its greater financial damage and lower media profile relative to street crime; victimless crime as a debated category; the UCR as the FBI's annual compilation of police-reported data from about 17,000 agencies and its failure to capture unreported crimes; the NCVS as a BJS self-report survey that records a higher rate of crime than the UCR; the long-term decline in crime rates since the early 1990s; and the finding that public perception of crime as high or worsening diverges from the data. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted. The book footer notes the book may not be ingested into LLMs without OpenStax's permission; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) — overview page
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. government primary source). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the NCVS as the nation's primary source of information on criminal victimization; the annual survey design (nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households; persons age 12 or older; administered by the U.S. Census Bureau for BJS); coverage of nonfatal personal crimes and household property crimes both reported and not reported to police; collection of victim, offender, and incident characteristics; exclusion of persons in institutions, military bases, and homeless populations; and the 2024 violent victimization rate of 23.3 per 1,000 persons age 12 or older (illustrative). Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: What the data says about crime in the U.S. (short read, April 24, 2024)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (Pew Research Center, live). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200); author John Gramlich. Supports: the FBI and BJS as the two primary sources of government crime statistics and the limits of each (FBI: reported crimes only, not all agencies participate; BJS: ages 12+, cannot count murder); 2022 FBI rates (1,954.4 property crimes vs 380.7 violent crimes per 100,000); long-term declines 1993-2022 (FBI violent -49%, property -59%; BJS -71% each) with the 2020 murder spike noted; perception gap (23 of 27 Gallup surveys since 1993 with at least 60% of adults saying national crime rose year over year, despite falling rates; community-level concern lower than national concern); demographic patterns (2022 BJS: younger and lower-income people more likely to report violent victimization); geographic patterns (2022 FBI: over 700 violent crimes per 100,000 in New Mexico and Alaska vs under 200 in Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Hampshire, and Maine); reporting rates (2022: 41.5% of violent and 31.8% of household property crimes reported; motor vehicle theft most reported at 80.9%; rape/sexual assault least at 21.4%); and reasons crimes go unreported. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.
